As the design progresses, the plan must be updated to reflect changes in scope, timeline, resources, or approach. Both 21 CFR 820.30(b) and ISO 13485 clause 7.3.2 require that the plan be reviewed and updated as the design evolves. The plan should be the project's main source for how design controls will be executed and actively managed throughout development. For example, the Design and Development Plan should serve as the top-level document and reference subordinate plans (verification plan, validation plan, risk management plan) for detail as evidence the full scope of design control activities has been planned, documented, and traceable.  Design decisions directly affect the well-being of device users and patients, FDA requires the manufacturer to maintain the knowledge base which forms a basis for the product design.  The DHF contains the records necessary to demonstrate that the design was developed in accordance with the approved design plan and the requirements of this part. The DHF, itself, is not part of the 510(k) submission application. Records (document output) from the DHF will be used as evidence in the 510(k) submission to support safety and effectiveness of the device. | ISO 13485 Subclause 7.1 requires the organization to plan and develop processes needed for product realization, including one or more risk management processes used in product realization and for records of these risk management activities to be maintained. | 820.30(b) Design and development planning. •  Each manufacturer shall establish and maintain plans that describe or reference the design and development activities and define responsibility for implementation. ·  The plans shall identify and describe the interfaces with different groups or activities that provide, or result in, input to the design and development process. ·  The plans shall be reviewed, updated, and approved as design and development evolves. |  |

In the usability engineering file for the coverage of IEC 62366-1:2020 clause 5.1 Prepare Use specification -a reference to the User Requirements / User needs is given which contains the section intended use.   Standard requirement. Patient profiles at greatest risk (e.g. pediatrics, neonates, pregnant women, …) need also to be explicitly specified. In case these populations are part of the intended use, extra review attention needs to be given to the artefacts that are related or derived from those intended use targets, more specifically: • Intended use: Description is provided that focuses on the medical purpose, medical indication of the product, process, or service, and medical procedure the device is used in. It is expected to include details on Intended User, Intended Use Environment and Operating Principle. • Intended Purpose / Indications for Use (equivalent term for respectively EU MDR and US): Description is provided for which use the device is intended according to the data supplied by the manufacturer on the labelling, in the instructions and/or in promotional material. It is expected to include details on patient populations and Indications. It is expected that the Intended Purpose / Indication for Use is either described as a separate chapter or as part of the Intended Use description. | Product Marketing Anita Makhija Gene Jagminas (Rick Dugan) | Daisy | D001555290_Rev C_VM13.0Epiq_URS | Operating principles are clearly described. | The Intended Use description does not contain all the required elements.   In summary: Population at greatest risk and contra-indications are not addressed in the Intended Use of referenced document. Intended medical indication, patient population, part of the body or tissue type interacted with, user profile and use environment are not explicitely described. More specifically:  1. Intended medical indication: The document states: "Sonography (ultrasonography) is widely used in medicine. It is possible to perform both diagnosis and therapeutic procedures." (Page 3, VP2024_URS-775) However, it does not specify particular medical indications (e.g., cardiac, abdominal, obstetric, etc.), but it refers in a general way to the use of transducers for specific medical usages.  2. Patient population: The document refers to "patients" in a general sense but no specific patient population (e.g., adults, pediatrics, neonates) is described. 3. Part of the body or tissue type interacted with: The document describes that "many ultrasound procedures are done using a transducer on the surface of the body," and also mentions specialty transducers for "endovaginal, endorectal, and transesophageal" use, as well as intravascular imaging. This indicates a wide range of body parts and tissue types, but does not mention them exhaustively. 4. User profile: The Intended use description does not provide a detailed user profile (e.g., radiologist, sonographer, physician, etc.) in the provided content. The text only implies that the user is a healthcare professional by the following sentence: “Users typically use a probe… read images from a screen”. 5. Use environment: The Intended use description does not provide a specific Use environment description. The text only implies that it is a clinical/medical setting where sonography is performed. 6. Population at greatest risk is not addressed in referenced document. 7. Contra-indications are not addressed in referenced document. | Complete | Y | Y | DI_1.1 | According to regulations the Intended Use shall be addressed as part of Design Input (according to FDA 21 CFR 820.30 (c) Design Input and ISO 13485 Clause 7.3.3). It should not be parceled in different documents/locations. |  | 21 CFR 820.30(c) states that “[e]ach manufacturer shall establish and maintain procedures to ensure that the design requirements relating to a device are appropriate and address the intended use of the device, including the needs of the user and patient.”   Design control begins with development and approval of design inputs. approval of design inputs,The indications for use describe the entire purpose for the medical device. This statement feeds into establishing user needs for the product. User needs initiate the design control process. User needs are the primary basis for establishing the design inputs.  Design input requirements must be comprehensive. Design input requirements fall under three categories: (1) Functional requirements (2) Performance requirements (3) Interface requirements.  For most medical devices, numerous requirements encompassing functions, performance, safety, and regulatory concerns are implied by the application. These implied requirements should be explicitly stated, in engineering terms, in the design input requirements. This makes it ppossible to assess whether the requirements completely characterize the intended use of the device.  ASSESSING DESIGN INPUT REQUIREMENTS FOR ADEQUACY (1) Design input requirements should be unambiguous. (2) Quantitative limits should be expressed with a measurement tolerance (3) The set of design input requirements for a product should be self-consistent. (4) The environment in which the product is intended to be used should be properly characterized. See column U.   clinical claims are explicit statements about device performance, safety, and benefits. These claims form the foundation of the clinical evaluation reports (CERs), regulatory submissions, and marketing materials. Each claim need specific supporting evidence from clinical studies, post-market surveillance data, or comparative analyses against state-of-the-art (SOTA) products. Cliinical claims should be specific, supported by robust evidence and align across all documentation. |  | Design input requirements must be comprehensive. Design input requirements fall under three categories: (1) Functional requirements (2) Performance requirements (3) Interface requirements.  For most medical devices, numerous requirements encompassing functions, performance, safety, and regulatory concerns are implied by the application. These implied requirements should be explicitly stated, in engineering terms, in the design input requirements. This makes it ppossible to assess whether the requirements completely characterize the intended use of the device.  ASSESSING DESIGN INPUT REQUIREMENTS FOR ADEQUACY (1) Design input requirements should be unambiguous. (2) Quantitative limits should be expressed with a measurement tolerance (3) The set of design input requirements for a product should be self-consistent. (4) The environment in which the product is intended to be used should be properly characterized. (5) When industry standards are cited, the citations should be reviewed for completeness and relevance. |  |

[X11-4t] [Ed Chan] Disagree Due to the nature of the TEE ultrasound transducer, many New, Unique, or Difficult (NUD) failure modes are inherently tied to the reliability requirements (as noted in the DFMEA) defined in the transducer specification document. The DFMEA is organized by mechanical structure because these elements drive how the requirements could fail. However, each failure mode is evaluated for its end effect against applicable safety requirements in the transducer specification document, including: -Fluid ingress/electrical energy exposure -Cleaning and sterilization compatibility -Edges and projections -Biocompatibility As a result, although structured mechanically, the DFMEA does assess failure modes based on their potential impact on safety. We can further improve clarity by explicitly cross-referencing failure modes to the corresponding safety requirement of the transducer specification document. (EPIQ)  finding is correct | Y | Y | Y |  |  | Y | H |  | In a technical review, a traceability matrix is utilized to identify “orphaned” requirements. If a Design Input exists without a corresponding Verification test, the design control process may be considered incomplete. Conversely, if a test is performed that does not map back to a specific Input or User Need, the necessity and relevance of that data may be questioned.  Creation of a traceability matrix is a fundamental component of the design control process for medical devices, critical to ensuring compliance with the US FDA regulations, specifically 21 CFR 820.30. The matrix links user needs to design inputs and integrates risk management practices as outlined by ISO 14971.   Objectives of a Traceability Matrix The primary objectives of developing a traceability matrix include: • Linking User Needs and Design Inputs: Ensuring that every user need is addressed by specific design inputs. • Facilitating Risk Management: Connecting each design input with associated risks, aligning with ISO 14971 requirements. • Verification and Validation Support: Providing a basis for conducting verification and validation activities. • Regulatory Compliance: Simplifying the process for audits and regulatory submissions by clearly demonstrating compliance with design control requirements. |  | 21 CFR 820.30(f) states that “[e]ach manufacturer shall establish and maintain procedures for verifying the device design. Design verification shall confirm that the design output meets the design input requirements. The results of the design verification, including identification of the design, method(s), the date, and the individual(s) performing the verification, shall be documented in the DHF.”  Verification means confirmation by examination and provision of objective evidence that  specified requirements have been fulfilled.  Design verification confirms that the product  developed is consistent with the assumptions made by the design team when developing design  inputs, but does not necessarily confirm that the product is safe and effective for its intended use.   Design verification activities may include, for example, performance tests, safety tests, or visual  inspections. |  |

The accuracy range list provided in 2004002343 is based on IEC 62354 and it is defining bare minumum for the measurement tools. It is good that the used tools are based on this list. However, this analysis is about whether the verification specification is defining the required test tool. A justification must be provided why certain tool is selected for a particular measurement. Such justification is missing in the documentation.  It is expected that the justification explains why certain type of tool is selected (due to electrical properties or due to limitations in the measurement area, etc) and whether the selected tool fits for the purpose; if there is a tolerance range given in the requirement, the selected tool must have better accuracy.  For the example given in column M, such a justification is expected: ''The requirement has an acceptance criteria of 1.0 +/-0.1mm. For this measurement, a Heindehain MT 60M Lenght Gauge is selected. Erdem, 27 May: The issue statement in coilumn M  is focusing on the lack of justification regarding the statement: ''Requirements referencing hardware that is unchanged from the prior verification of the VM platform will inherit the results from the prior verification program.'', and lack of justification whether the requirements related to critical operating points are affected by changes (even if it is only software). This finding is strenghtened with the footnote statements given in section 16.1 of System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0 D001881563: 1- This procedure tests software workflows that are common to EPIQ and Affiniti, and that are not dependent on the performance specifications of the hardware. This procedure can be tested on any supported hardware configuration (EPIQ C-cart. EPIQ B-cart, or Affiniti B-cart). 2- This procedure tests software workflows that are common to EPIQ and Affiniti, but that may perform differently depending on the performance specifications of the hardware. This procedure should be tested on EPIQ B-cart or Affiniti B-cart. This will test the worst case, since these two hardware configurations have the same CPU, which is lower-powered than the EPIQ C-cart CPU. 3- This procedure tests functionality only available on the EPIQ product. This tests software workflows that are not dependent on the performance specifications of the hardware. This procedure can be tested on EPIQ C-cart or EPIQ B-cart. 4- This procedure tests software workflows that have significant implementation differences on EPIQ and Affiniti. This procedure should be tested both on EPIQ (either C-cart or B-cart or both) and Affiniti B-Cart.  Footnotes further underpin the finding that software only updates can impact system performance because of hardware performance dependenciies. Therefore, the expectation is that a more detailed analysis is conducted and justification is provided regarding the ciritical operating conditions and worst case scenarios (can very well be limitations of the hardware in which the updated software is running) | Greg | READY TO CONNECT - EPIQ Verification (Balaji needed) | EPIQ Meeting Scheduled: 5-Jun-2026 | Y |  |  |  |  |  |  | Y |  |  |  |  |

Erdem, Arie, 11 May Expectation is that verification plan / protocol is reviewed/approved/released before the start of verification and that that the plan includes information on scope reduction of a protocol (if applicable) and that either the plan or protocol includes or references to the specific equipment to be used. If not done, the verificaiton plan/protocol has open ends which require decision of verification engineer. If done, this does not meet the intention of the regualtions / standards.  In Section 6.1 of QLAB 3DQ - US118B0823 - Epiq - VMQ - 13.0.0.1411, the test equiment are only defined as ''2D phantom, Flow phantom, ECG simulator with leads''. Instead of writing non-specifying information as ''test equipment'', the protocol must define the required details of the equipment.As an exampple: A specific model (defined by brand and model number) can be defined to be used in verification, e.g CIRS 3D Ultrasound Calibration Phantom Model 055, but it is also required to give a non-brand specific requirements of equipment/tool for at least two reasons: (1) tool requirements - derived for product requirement - are the starting point for tool / equipment selection / reliazed; (2) in case the defined device is not available at the moment of testing, an alternative device which meets the specifed technical requirements can be used. In the particular example, under discussion, neither a specific model of a tool is mentioned nor the required technical specifications of the tools is provided. Thus, it cannot be confirmed whether the used equipments like, ''Fluke ProSim 2 Vital Signs Simulator'' and ''CIRS 3D Ultrasound Calibration Phantom Model 055'' are technically suitable for the purpose of the test case. Bottom line is that neither the technical specifications of the needed test equipment nor ool tool justification for (not) using is it not provided. Because Subclause 7.3.10 requires a manufacturer to maintain its design and development files, FDA expects that those files will contain the necessary information to provide a full description of the design and development controls that are part of the QMS.  FDA recommends that submitters provide the following information as part of the manufacturer’s full description of its QMS in the marketing submission:   The plan for, and results of, the validation activities for design and development as described in Subclause 7.3.7. A full description would generally include: • A list of validation activities conducted and associated reports of results (these may be cross-references to other reports provided elsewhere in the application).  • Documentation that the design and development results will meet the requirements for the specified application or intended use(s).  • Documentation of validation plans that include methods, acceptance criteria, and as appropriate, statistical techniques with sample size/descriptions and supporting rationale.  • The design validation on representative product, which includes initial production units/batches or their equivalents, with:  • A rationale for the choice of product used for validation.  • The differences, if any, between the product used for validation and the device under review.  • A clear statement of limitations on the scope of the validation activities, for example, in cases where the validation was limited to a specific component.   • When a device is intended to be used as part of a system or with another device, the validation activities for the system or with the other device(s).  • Any other appropriate cross-references to information provided elsewhere in the application. Barbara van Nuland_ reply on disagree Doug (7 April 26): The validation protocol does not define acceptance criteria with sufficient specificity to consistently demonstrate, through objective evidence, that user needs and intended use requirements are met.  From an ISO 13485 and FDA design controls standpoint, validation activities are expected to be planned and documented such that conformance decisions are based on defined criteria rather than individual interpretation.  - ISO 13485:2016, clause 7.3.3 requires design and development inputs to be complete, unambiguous, verifiable/validatable, and not conflicting.   - ISO 13485:2016, clause 7.3.7 requires design and development validation to be performed under planned and documented arrangements to confirm the device is capable of meeting requirements for the specified application or intended use.   - 21 CFR 820.30(g)/ 21 CFR 820.3(z)(2) defines design validation as establishing by objective evidence that device specifications conform with user needs and intended uses.  In the current protocol, Section 6.4 includes a scoring scale (‑2 to +2). However, Section 6.3.2 does not define the criteria or decision rules for assigning “clinically unacceptable,” “acceptable,” or “exceeds expectations” for each test case. As a result, the scoring relies on reviewer judgement, and the basis for pass/fail determination is not sufficiently objective or consistently auditable. This indicates that the documented acceptance criteria are not adequately defined to support validation conclusions in alignment with ISO 13485:2016 clauses 7.3.3 and 7.3.7 and 21 CFR 820.30(g).  To address this, acceptance criteria can be strengthened by defining measurable thresholds and decision rules where feasible (e.g., accuracy limits, time-to-complete targets, image quality parameters, comparison/reference standards) and specifying the objective evidence to be recorded (e.g., screenshots, measured values, reviewer observations tied to a defined rubric, and explicit pass/fail rules). | Greg | READY TO CONNECT | Meeting Scheduled:  5-Jun-2026 | Y |  |  |  |  |  |  | Y |  |  |  |  |

X11-4 See finding reported on  D001873583 in DC_1.1  on confidence level . | Sampled | Y | Y | DC_1.3 | Sina, Arie, May 26:  Note 1: Following the FDA Guidance document "Deciding When to Submit a 510(k)", a design change to a medical device must always be evaluated through a risk-based assessment; this step cannot be skipped. The risk assessment is essential to identify any new risks or changes to existing risks, including potential impacts on device safety and effectiveness. Risk is assessed based on likelihood (probability) and severity of harm. A device modification that leads to a significant change in the device’s risk profile likely requires submission of a new 510(k). It is also possible that revewing dFMEA as the risk assessment, does not end up with up any change in dFMEA, but revewing it is necessary. Verification and validation testing are required; however, they serve only as a confirmation of the risk assessment outcome and do not replace it. Successful verification testing alone cannot demonstrate that a design change has no impact on effectiveness if the risk assessment indicates a potential effect. Therefore, a robust regulatory justification requires both an initial risk-based assessment showing no new or significantly modified risks, and verification results confirming no unexpected issues. Only when both elements support the same conclusion can it be documented that the design change does not significantly affect the device’s safety or effectiveness. Note 2: The document “2004001066 Design Controls_PROCESS FOR ELECTRICAL HARDWARE DEVELOPMENT” does not specify that an initial risk assessment is required for every design change, regardless of the change classification. | Design Transfer 21 CFR 820.30(h) 21 CFR820.250  7.3.8 Design and development transfer | • For those Design Outputs that are identified as essential, manufacturing controls are traced to essential design inputs in a risk-based approach. (see also Design Output 21 CFR 820.30(d) and ISO13485 Clause 7.3.4) • Sampling plans are in place to verify the acceptability of process capability written and based on a valid statistical rationale.  For those Design Outputs that are identified as essential which are translated into supplier part /production specifications:  • Parts / the results of a process are fully verified by subsequent inspection and test, or the process is validated.  • Parameters of qualified parts / process parameters for validated parts / processes are monitored and controlled to ensure that the specified requirements continue to be met. • Monitoring and control methods and data are recorded.  • Changes and part / process deviations are reviewed, and re-validation is performed and documented as appropriate. |  | DT_A1 | Review the Process Validation Plan/Report and Test Methods | DT_1.1 | Does the Process Validation Plan / Report addresses all essential design outputs ? | CtS/CtQ are used in PEPF as criticality classification to identify Essential Design Outputs (21 CFR820.30(d). Design transfer is the bridge between the design of the product and the manufacturing process to make the commercial product.  21 CFR 820.30(h)  ISO 13485 Subclause 7.3 and its subclauses describe the requirements for design and development controls. Because Subclause 7.3.10 requires a manufacturer to maintain its design and development files, FDA expects that those files will contain the necessary information to provide a full description of the design and development controls that are part of the QMS.  FDA recommends that submitters provide the following information as part of the manufacturer’s full description of its QMS in the marketing submission:  The procedures for the transfer of design and development outputs to manufacturing under Subclause 7.3.8. A full description would generally include:  • Procedures specific to the organizations responsible for each activity, including for in-house manufacturing and various contract manufacturers and component (or product) suppliers, as applicable, with:  • An explanation for how to transfer information about manufacturing controls and requirements to the different organizations.  • Procedures to ensure adequate transfer of design and development outputs that are essential to the safe and effective use of the device.  • Records of verification and approval of design outputs prior to transfer.  • Specifications for necessary infrastructure, equipment, personnel, and expertise.  • Plans for, and records of, equipment qualification, process validation, personnel training, and other setup activities.  • Sampling plans, equipment maintenance activities, cleaning procedures, and specifications for other ongoing/periodic quality control measures.  • Records of any review(s) to determine if transfer was effective and complete.  • Any appropriate checklists or trace matrices (or cross-references to information provided elsewhere in the application). |  |

Together policy and plan should cover together all aspects. It could also be that the two are combined. Policy and plan template from ARIS could be used to guide the assessment but consider that dependent on the chosen implementation information could be present in different formats. Focus should be on risk acceptability framework and risk acceptability criteria details, tables for quantiattaive ranges and qualitative levels for probability estimations, methodology to apply for establishing risk acceptability when probabilities cannot be estimated, generating the product safety risk profile, managing unacceptable risk, and considerations related to critical-to-safety and critical tasks. Also, Section 2.6 includes the software classification (Class C), and specified essential performance in Section 2.7 (Generate diagnostic CT X-ray image + Perform scanning for interventional procedure). • Section 3 of the Plan for Responsibilities and authorities includes roles, responsibilities and name of people fullfilling those roles. • Section 4 of the Policy and of the Plan include description of P1/P2/PoH's quantitative ranges and qualitative levels, and the methodologies followed for determination of the probability estimations. The method for estimating the PoH qualitative levels based on P1 and P2 qualitative levels is also included. • Section 4 of the Policy and of the Plan documents describes the approach to follow when P1 and/or P2 cannot be estimated. • Section 6.4 of the Plan  includes a description of risk management strategy for the product. • Section 8 of the Plan includes a comprehensive list of inputs into the Risk Management File. • Section 8.1 of the Policy details the risk reduction end point methodology. • The Policy details the methodology for identifying CTS/CT classifications in Section 9. • Sections 9 and 10 of the Plan describes the Risk Management activities occuring  in the Post Production phases, and the frequency with which the review of RMF and the PMS activities will be executed. | (1) Section 2 of the Policy does not list the Product(s)/Product Family(ies) in scope of the document. Boundaries help the entity owning product making sure the risk management is comprehensively covering the product and the interfacing of their product with other products. {PEPF 16.2.12.2 R24.9, Section 4.3; Risk Management Plan template R24.9, Sections 2 and 3} (3) The Plan includes only a brief and high-level product description and its intended use. It would have been expected to include device description and intended use based on EPIQ's 510(k) K182857. {Risk Management Plan Template R24.9, Section 3} (4) The Plan does not describe the product architecture, with mapping of product architectural elements to risk management elements (e.g., DFMEA mapped to subsystems or parts). {Risk Management Plan Template R24.9} (5) The safety-related characteristics, together with their ranges (where applicable), are not listed in the Plan. {ISO 14971, Clause 5.3} {PEPF 16.2.12.2 R24.9, Section 4} (6) The Policy and the Plan documents do not list or reference the specific clauses in the regulations and standards, the specific stakeholders and their concerns, and the State Of The Art that are applicable to the product. {PEPF 16.2.12.2 R24.9, Section 4.5; Risk Management Plan Template R24.9, Section 5.4.1} (7) The Policy and the Plan documents do not list or reference the specific risk acceptability criteria applicable to the product. {ISO 14971, Clause 4.4.d, A.2.7.3} {Risk Managemenet Plan Template R24.9, Section 5.4.1} (8) The product stakeholders are suggested only at high-level and in general and their concenrs are not specified in the Plan. It would have been expected to include, for example: American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine (AIUM); American Registry for Diagnostic Medical Sonography (ARDMS); European Federation of Societies for Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology (EFSUMB); European Society of Radiology (ESR); International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology (ISUOG); Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound (SRU); Medical Imaging & Technology Alliance, Ultrasound Section; Ultrasound Working Group, EFIM (European Federation of Internal Medicine), etc. {ISO 14971, Clause 4.2}  {PEPF 16.2.12.2 R24.9, Section 4.8} (9) The Plan does not detail the methodology for identifying the hazards associated with the product in a comprehensive and systematic manner, and how ther associated risks are being estimated, evaluated, controlled, and monitored. It would have been expected to describe methods used to identify hazards like: failure mode analyses, cybersecurity risk analyses, and any other types of analysis that may be applicable to the products/product families under scope of this plan (e.g. Safety Characterization Worksheet (to identify normal condition hazards), environmental impact analyses, sustainability analyses, AI/ML failure analyses, etc.). It would have been expected to describe the methodology for estimating risks (for each hazardous situation, estimating risk as a combination of the probability of occurrence of harm and the severity of harm for all foerseeeable sequeneces of events) and for evaluating risks (by comparing product estimated risks against predefined risk acceptability criteria to determine whether they are acceptable).  It would have been expected to describe the methodology for identification and implementation of risk control measures to reduce risk, then evaluating and considering their effectiveness in reducing risk. It would have been expected to describe the methodology for maintaining the medical device's risks during post-market by continuously collecting and analyzing safety data, updating the risk management file, and implementing corrective or preventive actions to ensure risks remain controlled and acceptable throughout the device lifecycle. {ISO 14971, Sections 5-7, and 10} {PEPF 16.2.12.2 R24.9, Section 4.5; Risk Management Plan Template R24.9, Section 5.1} (10) The methodology on how the product-related safety risk controls are verified for implementation is not documented in the Plan. It would have been expected to describe the methodology for verifying the implementation of the RCMs by confirming that each measure has been integrated into the device design, manufacturing process, labeling, or accompanying documentation. Verification is typically performed through a combination of: design output reviews confirming that requirements generated and traceable to RCMs are incorporated into technical specifications and design documents, inspection or tests to ensure physical or functional implementation (e.g., safety features, alarms, software constraints), document checks to confirm inclusion of labeling, instructions for use, and training materials as applicable. {ISO 14971, Clause 7.2} {Risk Management Plan Template R24.9, Section 6} (11) The methodology on how the product-related safety risk controls are verified for effectiveness is not documented in the Plan. A description of the methodology to establish the risk zones and their distribution throughout the risk profile based on risk status of the product is not included in the Plan. {PEPF 16.2.12.1 R24.9, Section 4.2} (21) Description of Zone 2 yellow  Safety Zone is inaccurate: "evaluate whether the benefits of the intended use outweigh the overall residual risks in this zone". It should be "evaluate whether the benefits of the intended use outweigh the individual residual risks in this zone". {PEPF 16.2.12.1 R24.9, Section 4.2} (22) The correct concept that the residual risk profile is "plotted with each uniquely identified hazard/hazardous situation combination" described in the PEPF 16.2.12.1 Risk Acceptability Criteria, has been replaced with the concept that the residual risk profile depicts "the distribution of the total number of Risk IDs", which may overlook risk aggregation. {PEPF 16.2.12.1 R24.9, Section 4.2} (23) The Policy and the Plan do no describe the methodology for estimating the residual risk for State Of The Art and for comparing the individual and the overall product residual risks with those of State Of The Art in order to ensure the risk acceptability. Additionally, SOTA is not detailed or referenced to where is detailed (expected in the Clinical Evaluation Report). {ISO 14971, Introduction, Clauses 3.28, 4.2, 10.3; ISO/TR 24971 Clauses 7.4.4, 8.3} (24) The Policy or the Plan do not specify the role the individual and overall BRDs are used to make the final determination of overall residual risk acceptability. {ISO 14971, Clause 8} {PEPF 16.2.12.2 R24.9, Section 4; Risk Management Plan Template R24.9, Sections 4.2 and 4.3} (25) The Policy or the Plan documents do not describe the approach to follow when individual or overall residual risks are determined to be unacceptable. [Derrick] INV13108 concluded that the failure was caused by use error and opened CR0116007 on 13-AUG-2024 as a possible enhancement to be implemented in the system. IMS team closed issue as No Planned Program on 21-AUG-2024 with the rationale: "PDMS team concludes the system is safe and effective for its intended use and closes this as No Planned Program."  Other products like Sparq and Flash have implemented this dialog as a Risk Control Measure as it was decided that the misunderstanding by the user could lead to the possibility of the machine not being available and lead to the potential of harm. Thus, I feel that the decision to write this as an enhancement and the rationale are both incorrect.  Cristian, 8 April: -PDMS acknowledged that “the failure was caused by use error.” Foreseeable use errors that can lead to safety hazards should be addressed within risk management in the same manner as hazards arising from failures or malfunctions, as all can result in hazardous situations and comparable risk to the patient. -Other products (Sparq, Flash) have implemented a Risk Control Measure (RCM) in the form of a user interface notification indicating that the system is in SLEEP mode. This reflects recognition that user misunderstanding may lead to device unavailability and potential harm.  If such an RCM is not implemented, or if it fails, the device may not deliver its intended use—whether due to use error, malfunction, or software-related issue—without the user being aware and able to intervene. This can result in delays in diagnosis or treatment and potentially lead to high-severity (S3–S4) harms. -Therefore, implementing this RCM in the Epiq product should not be considered an enhancement, but rather a necessary risk control to reduce the risk of loss of primary function. Without it, the risk is not reduced as far as possible.  While in the reported complaint the user ultimately recognized that the system was in SLEEP mode and restored functionality, the hazardous situation had already occurred: the device was not delivering its intended use as expected, and no information was provided to the user to indicate this condition. |  | Resolved | 21-Apr-2026, BRT/IRT meeting:  Finding has been discussed, agreed and concluded the issue is not an enhancement but a use/safety error, that risk is not reduced as far as possible (as demonstrated in other product) and defect should therefore be reassessed. | Y | Y | Y |  |  | Y | No | N/A | document update to address finding(s). |  |  |  |

FDA 2023 final guidance emphasizes importance of 62304 in the development of medical device software. FDA encourages the consideration of these guidances when developing device software functions and preparing premarket software documentation.  The new FDA guidance has simplified safety classification to Basic or Enhanced level of documentation, based on the safety risk of the software. In Section VI of the new guidance shows what software documents are required for each level. Importantly, software submissions to FDA now require the product’s full Risk Management File (plan, risk assessments, report, etc.) instead of just a “Device Hazard Analysis.” The new guidance also provides more detailed explanations of expected contents of each type of software documentation (Software Requirements Specification, Software Architecture, etc.).  IEC 62304 defines software architecture as the “organization and structure of the software system,” encompassing the software components and their interactions, as well as the context (hardware, other software, users) in which they operate.  Interfaces must be defined – both interfaces between software items and interfaces between the software and any external elements (e.g. hardware devices, user, network). | Adherence to IEC 62304 demonstrates compliance with general safety and performance requirements (GSPRs) | FDA software guidance is intended to provide information regarding the recommended documentation for premarket submissions for FDA’s evaluation of the safety and effectiveness of device software functions, which are software functions that meet the definition of a device under section 201(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act).  Manufacturers of device software must create and maintain software-related documentation in accordance with the requirements of the Quality System (QS) Regulation (21 CFR 820.30 Subpart C – Design Controls of the Quality System Regulation).  As part of QSR design controls, a manufacturer must “establish and maintain procedures for validating the device design,” which “shall include software validation and risk analysis, where appropriate” (21 CFR 820.30(g)).  FDA recognized IEC 62304 supports existing regulatory requirements ensuring that medical device software meets the same safety and performance requirements as its physical hardware. FDA 2023 final guidance emphasizes importance of 62304 in the development of medical device software. How these requirements of the 62304 standard are translated into specific procedures can vary considerably from company to company depending on the complexity of the software and the safety risks associated with it.  the new guidance describes information that would be typically generated and documented2 during software development, verification, and validation.  The new FDA guidance has simplified safety classification to Basic or Enhanced level of documentation, based on the safety risk of the software. In Section VI of the new guidance shows what software documents are required for each level. Importantly, software submissions to FDA now require the product’s full Risk Management File (plan, risk assessments, report, etc.) instead of just a “Device Hazard Analysis.” The new guidance also provides more detailed explanations of expected contents of each type of software documentation (Software Requirements Specification, Software Architecture, etc.).   Software Documentation Element Documentation Level Evaluation Software Testing as Part of Verification and Validation. A summary description of the testing activities at the unit, integration and system levels; PLUS nit and integration level test protocols including expected results, observed results, pass/fail determination, and unit and integration level test reports.  The following software testing documentation should be provided:  •  A summary description of the testing activities at the unit, integration, and system levels. The summary description should include the software version tested and the overall  pass/fail test results for all test protocols (i.e., collection of test procedures for specific software functionality executed. If the device is a modified version of a previously cleared or approved device, provide a summary of the modifications compared with the previous cleared or approved version along with a summary description of the additional testing activities performed at the unit, integration, and system levels as compared with the previously cleared or approved version.  Any intentional changes made in response to failed tests and documentation of test results demonstrating that the intentional changes were implemented correctly.   •  A regression analysis and regression testing with pass/fail test results (where applicable)  to account for unintended effects of a software change.  •  Regression analysis is a documented evaluation of the impact of a software change based on review of the relevant documentation (e.g., software requirements specification, software design specification, source code, test plans, test cases, test scripts, etc.) to determine whether regression testing is needed. If regression testing is needed as determined by the regression analysis, the sponsor should identify the necessary regression tests to be run. Regression testing is the rerunning of test cases that a program has previously executed correctly and comparing the current result to the previous result in order to detect unintended effects of a software change.  •  System level test protocol including expected results derived from software requirements, actual results that are observed and recorded, objective pass/fail determination (i.e.,actual results are acceptably equivalent to expected results) and a system level test report. The system level test report should demonstrate that the protocol has been acceptably executed with passing test results and any unresolved anomalies have been acceptably deferred based on a risk assessment for the candidate release version.  In addition to the documentation requested for the Basic Documentation Level, all unit and integration level test protocols and reports should be provided, including expected results derived from software requirements and design, actual results that are observed and recorded, and objective pass/fail determination (i.e., actual results are acceptably equivalent to expected  results). The unit and integration level test reports should demonstrate that the protocols have been acceptably executed with passing testing results and any unresolved anomalies have been acceptably deferred based on a risk assessment for the candidate release version.  below provides an outline of the recommended documentation for each software documentation element and corresponding Documentation Level. Documentation Level Evaluation A statement indicating the Documentation Level and a description of the rationale for that level.  Software Description Software description, including overview of significant software features, functions, analyses, inputs, outputs, and hardware platforms.  Risk Management File Risk management plan, risk assessment demonstrating that risks have been appropriately mitigated, and risk management report.  Software Requirements Specification (SRS) SRS documentation, describing the needs or expectations for a system or software, presented in an organized format, at the software system level or subsystem level, as appropriate, and with sufficient information to understand the traceability of the information with respect to the other software documentation elements (e.g., risk management file, software design specification, system and software architecture design chart, software testing).  System and Software Architecture Design Detailed diagrams of the modules, layers, and interfaces that comprise the device, their relationships, the data inputs/outputs and flow of data, and how users or external products (including information technology (IT) infrastructure and peripherals) interact with the system and software.  Software Design Specification (SDS) SDS documentation, including sufficient information that would allow FDA to understand the technical design details of how the software functions, how the software design completely and correctly implements all the requirements of the SRS, and how the software design traces to the SRS in terms of intended use, functionality, safety, and effectiveness.  Software Development, Configuration Management, and Maintenance Practices Basic Documentation Level, PLUS complete configuration management and maintenance plan document(s); OR A Declaration of Conformity37 to the FDA-recognized version of IEC 62304, including subclause 5.1 (Software development planning), clause 6 (software maintenance process), and clause 8 (software configuration management process), among others as applicable.  Software Testing as Part of Verification and Validation Basic Documentation Level, PLUS unit and integration level test protocols including expected results, observed results, pass/fail determination, and unit and integration level test reports.  Software Version History A history of tested software versions including the date, version number, and a brief description of all changes relative to the previously tested software version.  Unresolved Software Anomalies List of remaining unresolved software anomalies with an evaluation of the impact of each unresolved software anomaly on the device’s safety and effectiveness. |  |

Details: Below are some samples from RMM that support this statement: - User Documentation / Information for Safety forms the largest category of external mitigations. For example, under Risk MNA-01 (machine not available due to software failure), the RMM identifies VP2025 RMM_CV-2630: "The user manual shall have a recommendation for the users to have a backup system present during critical exams and TEE exams." This is a healthcare procedure-based mitigation external to the software. - Hardware watchdog and power monitor mechanisms are explicitly documented as external safety controls. For example, under Burn risk B-10, VP2025 RMM_CV-4674 states: "If the power monitor fails, the watchdog timer shall turn off all of the power supplied to all transducers except PPWR." The watchdog timer is an independent hardware mechanism that operates external to the software system. - Transducer hardware design specifications serve as external mitigations. For example, VP2025 RMM_CV-621 (Risk B-15) states: "Transducer assemblies shall have a patient contact surface temperature not exceeding 43°C when measured under test conditions per IEC 60601-2-37." This is a hardware design constraint, not a software control. - Thermistor-based thermal monitoring in TEE and XICE probes provides hardware-level external safety. VP2025 RMM_CV-1836 (Risk B-10): "TEE probes shall incorporate a thermistor in transducer, thermal management system with real time monitoring and control of PAP temperature, and fault detection." - Manufacturing and process controls are documented as external mitigations. VP2025 RMM_CV-1403 (Risk P-30): "Production processes for the system shall be specified in conformance with 9043-0526 Production Process Specification Protocol." VP2025 RMM_CV-4205 (Risk BG-10): "Biopsy guide suppliers shall be selected in conformance with 16.2.18.1 Supplier Selection, Classification and Approval." - Transducer manufacturing tolerances are hardware-external. VP2025 RMM_CV-2375 (Risk B-20): "Transducer output level is controlled such that there is a 90% confidence that 90% of all the transducers manufactured will not exceed the specified limits." | Summary: D001707530_Rev A, VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification: 7.3.13 section lists the severity to safety classification in alignment with 62304.  In the RMM, there is misalignment between severity and Software safety classification. These are of two types: 1. Lower software risk classification than justified by severity. 2. Higher software risk classification than justified by severity.  Alslo, in the RMM, there are risks (eg: MNA-85), where mitigations are not marked as "software related" but the mitigation steps clearly indicate that software is involved (show warning message to the user). Also, for these mitigations, there is no software risk classification (see in RMM, MNA worksheet, Rows: 80, 212, 234, columns N, O and P).  Examples are provided below: 1. The Machine Not Available (MNA) Anomalies This sample group represents risks where the initial risks are classified as high, the mitigations rely on software or alarms, and the software classification is set to a lower risk level.  Risk IDs: MNA-70, MNA-80, MNA-85, MNA-90 Initial Risk: 3 (Suggesting potential for Death or Serious Injury, expecting SW Class C). Hazard/Harm: Patient Exposure during Clinical Use leading to Distress, Injury, or Irritability.  Current SW Class: A What is the Anomaly: The mitigations for these risks are entirely software-based or informational. They include things like: - "When error conditions are such that there is no recovery mechanism... a message shall be displayed to the End-User" - "The user manual shall have a recommendation for the users to have a backup system present" - "When the system is using FPGA... and detects corrupt state, it shall perform a recovery within 2 seconds" - "System shutdown time shall not exceed 65 seconds" IEC 62304 Deviation (Clause 4.3): A software safety class cannot be lowered using a software-driven mitigation (like displaying an error message) or "Information for Safety" (like a user manual warning to have a backup system). IEC 62304 states that software failure probability is assumed to be 100%. If the software fails, it cannot warn the user, nor can it guarantee a 2-second recovery. Without an external, independent hardware interlock preventing the harm, the expectation is that this software remains Class C.  Risk ID: MNA-06 Initial Risk: 2 (Expecting SW Class B). Current SW Class: A What is the Anomaly: Similar to the above, this risk classification was lowered from B to A. Without a hardware mitigation, it is not expected to be lowered to Class A.  2. The Misdiagnosis (MD and MDQ) Lowered Anomalies This sample group identifies incorrect diagnostic information directly impacts clinical decision-making.  Risk ID: MD-35 Initial Risk: 3 (Death/Serious Injury, anticipating SW Class C). Current SW Class: B What is the Anomaly: The mitigations include software operations:  - "When the system transitions from Dual to a new imaging mode, the system shall apply the pertinent settings for the new imaging mode." IEC 62304 Deviation: The hazard here carries a severity of 3 (Class C). The mitigation relies on the software correctly applying new settings when transitioning modes. If the software fails to do this (which IEC 62304 assumes it will), the user is presented with incorrect settings, which could lead to misdiagnosis. Because the mitigation is in the software itself, it is not considered sufficient to reduce the software safety class from C to B.  Risk ID: MD-4015 Initial Risk: 3 (Death/Serious Injury, anticipating SW Class C). Current SW Class: B What is the Anomaly: The mitigations are purely computational software requirements: - "For every transducer that supports PW Doppler, PW Doppler Spectral mean Velocity accuracy shall display with an accuracy of ≤15% error..." IEC 62304 Deviation: A requirement stating that the software *must be accurate* does not serve to mitigate the risk of the software *being inaccurate*. Since an inaccurate display can lead to serious injury/misdiagnosis (Initial Risk 3), the software calculating and displaying this velocity is expected to be classified as Class C. Classifying it as B bypasses the more rigorous architectural and testing standards required for critical diagnostic algorithms.  Risk ID: MDQ-55 (QLab Misdiagnosis) Initial Risk: 3 (Death/Serious Injury, anticipating SW Class C). Current SW Class: B What is the Anomaly: The mitigations rely on the Q-App software refusing to open uncalibrated images (e.g., "The a2DQ Q-App shall not open the following uncalibrated images..."). IEC 62304 Deviation: The mitigation is a software check. If the software fails, it might accidentally open and process an uncalibrated image, which could lead the clinician to make a diagnostic error. Because the safeguard is written in software, the expectation is that the software itself must be Class C.  3. The "Raised" Anomalies (Architectural Mingling) This sample group are not a strict safety concerns, but they demonstrate a deviation from the expected mapping and may indicate architectural inefficiencies.  Risk IDs: - MNA-170 (Machine Not Available): Initial 1 ➔ SW Class B - MD-3030 (Misdiagnosis): Initial 1 ➔ SW Class B (Mitigation: "Displayed scaling indicators shall accurately correspond...") - WH-10, WH-20 (Wireless): Initial 1 ➔ SW Class B (Mitigations: Restarting jobs, whitelisting AVS software, hiding PHI). - MDQ-20, MDQ-170 (QLab): Initial 2 ➔ SW Class C (Mitigations: Allowing user to accept/reject borders and measurements). - P-30 (Process): Initial 1 ➔ SW Class B   What is the Anomaly: In all these cases, the assigned Software Class is higher than the Initial Risk severity would dictate.  IEC 62304 Implication (Clause 4.3.d): This occurs when low-risk software functions (like handling Wi-Fi drops, displaying simple scaling indicators, or allowing a user to click "Accept") are bundled into the same software architecture as high-risk items (like the core imaging calculations) without adequate segregation.  The Burden: Because they are not segregated, these low-risk items "inherit" the higher safety class of the overarching system. While this is safe, it means the engineering team must apply Class B or Class C documentation, unit testing, and architectural rigor to simple features like Wi-Fi reconnection logic or UI buttons, which can require significant development time and resources. | Sample  (Random sampling of SOUP/OTS software) | Y | Y | SW_1.4 | [Qifeng] Agree with Issue Statement finding. |  | Agree |  | Y | Y | Y |  |  | Y | H | N/A | Clause 4 states the following rule: if a hazardous situation could arise from a failure of the software, the probability of that failure is assumed to be 100%. This includes 2D measurement tools (distance, area, circumference), M-mode and Doppler measurement tools, OB calculations (fetal age, growth, estimated fetal weight), Cardiac analysis (ejection fraction, wall motion, strain), Vascular measurements, data accuracy tolerances, and algorithmic error limits. (Addresses Arie's Q4: The ARS requests specific software calculations and features. The SSRS (D001592303) requires execution and tracking of physical "Hardware Tests" and "Hardware Versions". Details: Here are some examples of well written requirements that have well-defined and testable criteria:  - All three major specifications (SWRS, ARS, SSRS) use numeric thresholds that support only one interpretation:   o SWRS examples: "12.5 MSamples per sec" (VP2024_SRS-62720), "1GB" (VP2024_SRS-40767), "2200 frames" (VP2024_SRS-47486), "0.XX precision" (VP2024_SRS-37106)   o ARS examples: "+/- 5%" (VP2024_ARS-131225, VP2024_ARS-131250 approx), "+/- 9%/±5%" (VP2024_ARS-131096), "1 decimal point precision" (VP2024_ARS-1451)   o SSRS examples: "within 10 seconds" (SSRS-278), "between 6 and 63" characters (SSRS-1157), "5 minutes/10 minutes/20 minutes/30 minutes/60 minutes" (SSRS-116 through SSRS-120)  - Every quantified attribute above defines a pass/fail criterion:    - ±5% accuracy: measure, compare to reference, check error ≤ 5%    - ≤12.5 MSamples/sec: measure data rate, compare to threshold    - ≤1GB: create export, check file size    - Within 10 seconds: trigger event, measure latency    - Password length [6..63]: attempt boundary-value passwords  -Monitored and/or Controlled by software:   - **Controlled examples**: data rate limiting (VP2024_SRS-62720), file size capping (VP2024_SRS-40767), measurement accuracy computation (VP2024_ARS-131225), password length enforcement (SSRS-1145/1157), auto-logoff timeout enforcement (SSRS-113)   - **Monitored examples**: latency logging (VP2024_SRS-62721), frame rate display (VP2024_SRS-2699: "shall provide the capability to display the systems actual frame rate value"), MI precision display (VP2024_SRS-37106) | Summary: The presence of subjective, optional, and unbounded requirements within the Software System Requirementsprevents objective Verification and Validation (V&V) for those requirements.   Based on random sampling from the referenced documents, here are 4 potential categories of findings that are non-compliant to the expectations of IEC 62304. For each category at least 1 illustrative example, including an explanation why it is not meeting the expectations, is provided below:  1. Untestable Qualitative Semantics ("Optimized")    - Evidence: `VP2024_SRS-908` states: "The M-Mode Color Flow shall be optimized to detect and display blood motion." Furthermore, `QLab2017_SRS-1144` states: "The Auto Area algorithm shall be optimized for hyper-echoic images. [Goal]"    - Why this is a finding: "Optimized" is a subjective quality. A Verification protocol cannot objectively prove a feature is "optimized," leading to "Pass" determinations based solely on tester opinion rather than engineering metrics. This directly violates the regulatory requirement for unambiguously testable software specifications.  2. Use of Optional Language ("Should" vs "Shall")    - Evidence: `VP2024_SRS-9109` states: "The number of scan lines should be optimized to the transducer performance..." Furthermore, `VP2024_ARS-65` states: "...measurement tools should support both automatic and user specified inputs." and `QLab2017_SRS-2360` states: "(3) QLAB should support the use of Multi-Planar Reformatting..."    - Why this is a finding: In standard regulatory and engineering syntax, "should" indicates a recommendation, whereas "shall" indicates a mandatory requirement. If a performance attribute is critical, writing it as "should" means it technically does not have to be implemented, leaving a loophole that is non-compliant with strict software requirement definitions, resulting in the possibility that design output is not meeting design input.  3. Unbounded Operational Scope ("Different states")    - Evidence: `VP2024_SRS-731` states: "The system shall be optimized for different blood flow states." Furthermore, `QLab2017_SRS-3784` states: "All the different ROIs in the ROI Q-App shall produce color index results."    - Why this is a finding: "Different blood flow states" defines an infinite scope. Under IEC 62304, requirements must be testable; this phrasing leaves it ambiguous which states are required (e.g., turbulent flow, low flow, pathological flow, how many states total). A requirement with infinite scope means the verification testing is inherently incomplete.  4. Failure to Decompose Ambiguity During System-to-Software Translation    - Evidence: The ambiguous phrases noted above were found traversing both the system baseline and the lower-level software specifications identically.     - Why this is a finding: While high-level system needs are occasionally broad, the software requirement is expected to resolve that ambiguity into actionable software code logic. The fact that the software specifications (SWRS, QLab SRS, ARS) simply repeat the vague statements indicates a failure in software design definition. | Sample  (Random sampling of SRS and SWRS, this does not represent the complete list of requirements that satisfy/do-not-satisfy the ask of the question) | Y | Y | SW_2.3 | [Qifeng] Agree with Issue Statement finding, some of these are legacy  requirements created a long time ago, we introduced new process and  made huge improvements better defining  system requirements in recently NPIs. |  | Agree |  | Y | Y | Y |  |  | Y | H | N/A | The FDA QSR requires “a mechanism for addressing incomplete, ambiguous, or conflicting requirements.”  Each requirement identified in the software requirements specification should be traceable and we recommend that the SRS be evaluated for accuracy, completeness, consistency, testability, correctness, and clarity. | Adherence to IEC 62304 demonstrates compliance with general safety and performance requirements (GSPRs) |  |  |

Details and Evidences: Based on random sampling from the referenced documents, here are 2 potential categories of findings that are non-compliant to the expectations of IEC 62304.  1. Lack of Verifiable Software Reliability Metrics    - Evidence: `VP2024_SRS-15823` defines reliability as "the total customer Emergency service Call (EMC) rate."     - Why this is a finding: An EMC rate is a lagging commercial KPI, not a software design input. A Verification Engineer cannot run a test protocol during development to prove the future field EMC rate. IEC 62304 expects non-functional requirements to provide proactive constraint on code stability (e.g., memory management limits, thread safety rules, maximum exception recovery times).  2. Unenforceable RAMS "Goals"    - Evidence: `VP2024_SRS-45189` "The system should be designed... such that the projected field service call rate is no less than 320 days... [Goal]" and `VP2024_SRS-45925` states the system "should" execute a self-test in under 15 minutes, labeled as a "[Goal]".    - Why this is a finding: As established in finding SW_2.3(3) regarding optional language, categorization as a "[Goal]" or phrasing with "should" is strictly unenforceable. In a highly regulated environment, a "Goal" cannot result in a "Fail" verdict during V&V if missed. If a self-diagnosis takes e.g. 30 min, in the field during a critical trauma case, it poses a clinical risk, yet the verification pass would be technically granted because 15 minutes was just a target. This violates the expectation that SOUP requirements must act as verifiable design inputs governing the software lifecycle.  Details: 1. Absence of SOUP Requirements in Software Specification Documents (IEC 62304 - 5.3.3 / 5.3.4)    - Evidence: Exhaustive text searches across the `Epiq_VM13.0_SWRS`, `Epiq_VM13.0_ARS`, `Voyager_Platform_13.0_SSRS`, and both QLAB specifications reveal zero inclusion of specific, functional, or performance requirements governing SOUP items or their explicit hardware/software prerequisites.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 implies that functional, performance, and prerequisite constraints for SOUP must be established as formal software requirements. Documenting them solely in an external "Assessment Checklist" means they do not flow into the standard traceability matrix (RTM). If a SOUP requirement isn't in the SWRS, it cannot be formally traced to an architectural component or a dedicated, automated software unit test.  2. Absence of SOUP Considerations in Architectural and Planning Documents    - Evidence: The `Project Management Plan`, `Software Development Plan`, and `VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification` fail to define how SOUP requirements constrain the software architecture or how SOUP components interface defensively with natively developed code.    - Why this is a finding: By separating SOUP analysis into a standalone checklist rather than integrating it into the core Software Design Specification, the architecture fails to demonstrate how it handles potential anomalous behavior, error messaging, or resource exhaustion triggered by the third-party libraries.  3. Missing SOUP-Specific Verification Strategies    - Evidence: Neither the `IntegDev Test Plan` nor the `System Verification Plan` outlines a test approach specifically designed to challenge the boundaries, error-handling capabilities, or performance thresholds of the integrated SOUP components.    - Why this is a finding: Verification plans that only test the monolithic system (e.g., "Did the image appear?") cannot implicitly verify the complex, underlying safety constraints of a standalone SOUP library. Without explicit SOUP requirements in the SWRS driving explicit SOUP test protocols in the Verification Plan, the rigorous V&V of third-party software cannot be proven.  4. Details: 1. Feature-Associated EDO Flows Not Addressed    - Evidence: The D001707530 Safety Risk Mitigations appendix explicitly covers only four systemic safety-mitigated requirements not related to a specific system feature (VP2024_SRS-1710, VP2024_SRS-24335/VP2024_SRS-24302, VP2024_SRS-24306). The reviewed documents do not contain equivalent data/information flow descriptions for feature-associated Essential Design Outputs (CTQ/CTS).    - Why this is a finding: The four systemic safety-mitigated requirements represent an extremely small fraction of the total safety-related software mitigations/requirements. The bulk of EDOs are associated with specific clinical features, and their data flow pipelines through the software architecture are not described in D001707530 or D001750035.  2. Software Units Not Defined at the Lowest Level    - Evidence: D001707530 names DLLs and executables (e.g., AnnotSPDll.dll, borisCore.dll, fccserver.dll) and decomposes the signal path into four subsystems. Neither D001707530 nor D001750035 defines software units at the lowest level per IEC 62304, nor allocates the named DLLs and executables to such units.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 expects software units to be defined at the lowest level of decomposition. Without defined units, DLL and executable names cannot be traced to a formal architectural element, and data/information flows for EDOs cannot be understood down to the lowest level of the software architecture.  3. Absent Control Flow Constraints for EDOs    - Evidence: D001707530 describes a generic publish-subscribe mechanism via VDB for signal path state updates and a transaction processing mechanism in Ultrasound Control. The Safety Risk Mitigations appendix describes data flow for scaling indicators (VP2024_SRS-24335/VP2024_SRS-24302) and temporal alignment (VP2024_SRS-24306) but does not specify conditional triggers, state transitions, or timing governing those hand-offs.    - Why this is a finding: The architecture defines the communication pattern but not the specific conditions under which safety-critical data is moved, leaving the control flow implicit rather than explicitly constrained for each EDO.  4. Implicit Safety Boundaries in Data Flow Descriptions    - Evidence: D001750035 Section 5.3 Functional Data Flow (Figure 2) and D001707530 Signal Path Services section describe data pathways between subsystems without distinguishing between safety-critical and standard operational data flows.    - Why this is a finding: The reviewed documents do not explicitly label or visually separate safety-critical data pathways from standard data pathways, leaving safety boundaries implicit in the architectural descriptions. | Sample | Y | Y | SW_3.2 | [Kevin] Disagree. Essential Design Outputs for Software FDA 21 CFR 820.30(d) and ISO 13485:2016 clause 7.3.4 require that design outputs:  ▪ Be documented in terms that allow adequate evaluation of conformance to design inputs ▪ Contain or reference acceptance criteria. ▪ Identify essential outputs for proper device functioning. ▪ Be reviewed, approved, and released with documented date and signature  For software, essential design outputs include:  ▪ Software Design Specification (SDS) — the primary output of the software detailed design proces ▪ Software Requirements Specification (SRS) — linking functional and non-functional requirements to architecture. ▪ Interface specifications between software and hardware, other software, and user interfaces. ▪ Acceptance criteria for software functions, including test cases and verification methods. ▪ Traceability matrix from requirements to design outputs and test cases. | Adherence to IEC 62304 demonstrates compliance with general safety and performance requirements (GSPRs) |  |  |

For submission filed after June 14, 2023 FDA guidance Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions shall be taken into account. | Systems Engineering Qifeng | Subramanya Vellal, Dattatreya | D001707530_Rev A_VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification D001750035_Rev A_VoyagerSystemDesignSpecification  Note: Assessment in line entries SW_1.1 through SW_10.4 is scoped to VM13 and QLab components only, and does not include all other components that are part of the EPIQ 13 SBOM. | Summary: The VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification defines limited software-level constraints for certain platform software items, demonstrating that the concept of data limits is captured at the software architecture level for those items.  Details: 1. Cineloop Memory Allocator Bounds    - Evidence: D001707530 states: "Cineloop during live imaging is allowed 15 seconds of data (translating to 30 slices, or 960 MB). It would start with one slice and then grow until it hit 30 slices in use, at which point it would release its oldest slice."  2. Image Display Maximum    - Evidence: D001707530 states: "The system is capable of having up to four native images or composite loops displayed at a time, or up to four composite still frames. These constraints come from memory, bus bandwidth, and CPU resource limits." | Summary: The reviewed software design documents do not systematically define quantified data ranges, limits, or accepted values for software items handling Essential Design Output parameters. Where constraints are present, they address platform-level resource bounds rather than EDO-specific acceptance criteria. A recurring pattern is the deferral of operational parameter boundaries to runtime configuration data, with no software-layer hard limits established within the software item designs themselves. No evidence exists in the design documentation that acceptance criteria for data values were derived from an architecture or detailed design analysis of Essential Design Outputs.  Details: 1. Data Range Not Adopted as a Software Design Specification    - Evidence: D001707530 states for the Replay Control software item: "The rate control may vary in the range given in the SRS." The document separately states: "One system requirement is to replay images at the rate they were acquired. Another is to vary the playback rate from 1/16 to 2 times the capture rate." The 1/16x to 2x range is attributed to the SRS rather than established as an output of architectural design analysis. D001707530 does not specify how the Replay Control software item or its sub-components enforce, validate, or bound that range. By contrast, D001707530 does specify an enforcement mechanism in one isolated instance: "AppUI invoking a 'mode change' request from USI can expect that request to complete in 100 ms per the requirements in the System Design Specification, and so would wait with a 200 ms timeout." Here a specific component (AppUI) is identified as the enforcer, a derived design value (200 ms = 2x the 100 ms requirement) is established, and the enforcement mechanism (timeout on asynchronous call) is explicit. This pattern is not applied to the Replay Control playback rate range or to any other operational data range in D001707530.    - Why this is a finding: Under IEC 62304 Clause 5.4.2, the detailed design must contain enough detail to allow correct implementation of each software unit, and under Clause 5.4.3, interfaces must be detailed enough to implement each software unit correctly. D001707530 attributes the playback rate range to the SRS but does not specify which component enforces it or how. The timeout example demonstrates that D001707530 is capable of specifying enforcement mechanisms for quantitative limits, but does so in only one isolated instance. Combined with the absence of defined software units at the lowest level, there is no design baseline that establishes the enforcement mechanism for the playback rate range boundary or any other operational data range.  2. No Systematic Data Range Definition for Software System Inputs and Outputs    - Evidence: Neither D001707530 nor D001750035 contains a systematic or consolidated definition of data ranges and accepted values for software system inputs and outputs. Parameters such as quantification output value bounds, measurement precision limits, and display acceptance ranges are not defined as explicit acceptance criteria in the reviewed design documents. Furthermore, Essential Design Outputs (CTQ/CTS) are not identified in the software requirements, meaning EDO-specific data ranges cannot be traced from requirements through to design.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 Clause 5.2.2 item b expects software system inputs and outputs to be defined with their ranges, limits, and data definitions. The reviewed design baseline does not contain evidence that data ranges for software system inputs and outputs were systematically analyzed or documented. The absence of identified EDOs at the requirements level compounds this gap, as it prevents the design from defining EDO-specific data range acceptance criteria even if it intended to.  3. Operational Parameter Boundaries for Safety-Sensitive Software Items Deferred to Runtime Configuration    - Finding: The VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification establishes that the software architecture resolves operational parameter ranges at runtime through its Plugin/VDB system, where plugins compute values based on transducer-dependent configuration data loaded at runtime. The VoyagerSystemDesignSpecification identifies user-adjustable parameters such as Gain, Power, M-Line position, and Sample Volume Size and Position as signal path controls, but neither design document defines software-level hard boundary values that the software items independently enforce for these parameters. No architecture-defined upper or lower limit for these controls is documented in the software design baseline.    - Why this is a finding: The software design relies entirely on the integrity of runtime configuration data to bound the values that safety-sensitive software items accept. Under the expectation for SW_3.3, acceptance criteria for data values that software items will accept should be the result of design analysis particularly of Essential Design Outputs. The absence of architecture-defined hard limits means that the software design does not establish an independent safety guardrail that would operate if the external configuration data were incorrect or outside intended bounds. | Sample | Y | Y | SW_3.3 | [Qifeng] Disagree. IEC 62304 Clause 5.2.2(b) expects software system inputs and outputs to be defined with their ranges, limits, and defaults.
