Details: 1. The VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification (Domain Model section, Information and Data Model View) explicitly identifies data analysis as a software function. It defines Measurement as the "generation of physical quantities by an analysis of properties of the data stream itself" (e.g., peak Doppler velocity from Doppler data, heart rate from ECG data), and defines Analysis Result as "the output of the analysis algorithms on measurement data," described as "clinically significant computations that assist the physician's diagnosis." 2. The VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification (Ultrasound Layer section, Plug-In Library sub-section) describes the Plug-In Library architecture as the mechanism for implementing the ultrasound Theories of Operation (THOPs). Each THOP is encapsulated as a self-contained plug-in algorithm with formally defined input/output boundaries: plug-ins may only read from the VDB and write outputs to the VDB. The plug-in executor automatically sequences algorithmic execution based on declared data dependencies. This establishes a structured, well-defined architectural framework for analysis algorithm execution within the software. | Summary: While the design documentation establishes that the software performs analysis of clinical data and describes the architectural framework for algorithm execution, neither the VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification nor the VoyagerSystemDesignSpecification describes the specific analysis methodologies applied by the individual algorithms. The design acknowledges that algorithms implement ultrasound Theories of Operation but does not document nor include by reference what those methodologies are, how they were selected, or what evidence supports their appropriateness for the clinical computations they perform.  Details: 1. Analysis Algorithms Acknowledged but Methodologies Not Described in Design Documents    - Finding: The VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification (Ultrasound Layer section, Plug-In Library sub-section) identifies that the Plug-In Library encapsulates ultrasound Theory of Operations (THOP) algorithms and that these algorithms compute clinically significant analysis results. However, the document does not describe nor include by reference the methodology of any individual algorithm. The architecture treats algorithmic content as opaque — inputs and outputs are defined through the VDB, but the analytical method, mathematical basis, or clinical rationale underpinning each algorithm is not documented within the reviewed design baseline.    - Why this is a finding: The question requires not only that the software performs analysis, but that the analysis methodology has been described and that evidence for the applied methodology has been provided. The reviewed design documents satisfy neither sub-condition for any individual analysis algorithm. Describing the architectural wrapper around algorithms is not equivalent to describing the methodologies the algorithms implement.  2. No Evidence of Applied Methodology Provided in Design Documentation    - Finding: Neither the VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification (across its Component Architecture, Information and Data Model View, and Safety Risk Mitigations sections) nor the VoyagerSystemDesignSpecification provides evidence or references to evidence  — such as validation studies, references to published scientific literature, or clinical verification data —  for the analysis methodologies applied by the software items performing clinical computations (e.g., peak Doppler velocity calculation, heart rate derivation, acoustic output computation).    - Why this is a finding: The expectation for this assessment question states that evidence for the applied methodology must be provided. This aligns with FDA guidance on Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions (applicable to submissions after June 14, 2023), which requires description and substantiation of the analytical approach used by device software. The absence of documented evidence for the methodologies in the design baseline leaves this expectation unaddressed. | Sample | Y | Y | SW_3.4 | [Qifeng] Disagree, SPDS/SDS are high level system design specs,  the individual feature algorithm is captured in FDSs/CDs. For submission filed after June 14, 2023 FDA guidance Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions shall be taken into account. | Systems Engineering, Clinical Affairs Andrew Yoo,  Asha Jacob | Subramanya Vellal, Dattatreya | D001707530_Rev A_VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification D001750035_Rev A_VoyagerSystemDesignSpecification D001808022, AutoMeasure v3 Study Report for protocol 300557_Rev.B D001808023_A_CSR_R-trigger Study_300556_FINAL  Note: Assessment in line entries SW_1.1 through SW_10.4 is scoped to VM13 and QLab components only, and does not include all other components that are part of the EPIQ 13 SBOM. | Summary: The reviewed design and clinical study documents confirm that AI/ML-enabled applications are present in the VM13 platform. For the R-trigger AI-based algorithm and the AutoMeasure v3 AI detection algorithm, the reference populations and study samples have been explicitly defined, and potential biases and limitations have been identified and addressed within their respective clinical study reports.  Details: 1. The AutoMeasure v3 Study Report (D001808022) and the R-trigger Study Report (D001808023) both explicitly define the reference populations and study samples used to validate the AI algorithms. The studies sampled adult subjects (18 years of age and above) from multiple institutions across the USA, Asia, and Europe. Demographics are explicitly defined (e.g., broad racial representation, mean age of 59.00 ± 16.66, and mean BMI of 28.85 ± 7.06), demonstrating a diverse sampling intended to represent the intended clinical population. 2. Both study reports explicitly identify and address potential biases and limitations through documented mitigation strategies and clinical requirements. Bias mitigation included blinding the technical leads to the clinical ground truth and subject demographics during processing, ensuring that the test data used in the validation studies were completely independent and distinct from the data used for AI algorithm development/training, and intentionally sampling a broad demographic distribution to mitigate population bias. Limitations were addressed by defining strict clinical requirements for the evaluable samples, such as requiring patients to be in sinus rhythm during acquisition and excluding cases with arrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation or ectopic heartbeats). 3. The VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification (Applications Layer section) also identifies the AI Breast Application as a distinct AI/ML-enabled software component within the Voyager platform. | Summary: While the clinical study reports provide comprehensive definitions of reference populations and address biases for the R-trigger and AutoMeasure v3 AI algorithms, the software design documentation does not systematically capture or cross-reference these AI/ML model characteristics. Furthermore, for the AI Breast Application identified in the software architecture, there is no corresponding documentation defining its reference populations, samples, biases, or limitations within the reviewed baseline.  Details: 1. AI/ML Model Characteristics and Populations Absent from Core Design Documentation    - Finding: Although the Clinical Study Reports for AutoMeasure v3 and R-trigger successfully define reference populations and bias mitigations, these characteristics are not documented or cross-referenced within the VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification or VoyagerSystemDesignSpecification. The architecture documents do not systematically capture the foundational AI/ML model characteristics, training approaches, or intended populations for the AI components they integrate.    - Why this is a finding: The expectation requires that foundational model characteristics for AI/ML applications are documented as part of the design baseline. Relying entirely on external clinical study reports without architectural cross-references leaves the software design baseline incomplete regarding the AI/ML models it encapsulates.  2. Missing Reference Populations and Bias Identification for the AI Breast Application    - Finding: The VoyagerSoftwarePlatformDesignSpecification (Applications Layer section, AI Breast Application sub-section) provides only a platform-integration description of the AI Breast Application. Neither the design documents nor any referenced clinical study reports define its reference populations, sample sets, potential biases, or limitations. The model architecture, training approach, inference method, and performance characteristics are not documented within the reviewed design baseline.    - Why this is a finding: The expectation requires that reference populations or samples are defined and biases addressed for all AI/ML-enabled applications. The absence of this documentation for the AI Breast Application leaves a gap in the design and validation baseline for this specific feature. | Sample | Y | Y | SW_3.5 | 1. Details: 1. Exploration of Hardware Variability and Performance Limits    - Evidence: D001596655 DFMEA VM13.0 Software Work For CV Optimization includes hardware-dependent failure modes such as incorrect cart configuration selection causing instability and data-rate cap failures leading to latency with potential patient safety impact for TEE probes. D001580585 VM13.0 DFMEA OnTheFlyForVm includes coefficient-calculation and state-setup failures interacting with hardware behavior, including the end effect "Transducer overheating and burning the patient." D001597673 DFMEA VM13.0 GpuSignalPathImprovements further analyzes excessive CPU loading, excessive GPU loading, dropped volumes, corrupted volume rendering, and GPU exception behavior leading to crash, reboot, or loss of diagnostically significant information.  2. Exploration of External System and External Data Interactions    - Evidence: D001580585 VM13.0 DFMEA OnTheFlyForVm identifies failure caused by the ATI server not pushing the correct state setup, resulting in generated transmit parameters that do not match the system state. D001580596 VM13.0 DFMEA EpmJson QF analyzes malformed or modified preset and quicksave files, missing files, corrupted files, disk errors, and import or restore media faults, including crash and patient-harm end effects. D001602384 VM13 DFMEA OneCollabLive analyzes environment issues such as folder access violations, file-in-use errors, unavailable ports used by another process, corrupted configuration or data files, and audit-trail library failures.  3. Exploration of Internal Software Element Interactions    - Evidence: D001596655 DFMEA VM13.0 Software Work For CV Optimization captures internal resource exhaustion and delayed UI response caused by CPU loading problems. D001579178 DFMEA VM13.0 Static 3D Markers models internal state and UI interaction failures such as Z-order widget conflicts and incorrect handling of state or mode transitions. D001597673 DFMEA VM13.0 GpuSignalPathImprovements analyzes internal data-path interactions where dropped or inconsistent frames propagate into slice-order corruption, timeouts, CUDA illegal-address failures, and non-graceful recovery behavior.  4. Presence of Traced Mitigations and Verification References    - Evidence: D001580596 VM13.0 DFMEA EpmJson QF links corrupted preset and quicksave scenarios to requirement VP2024_SRS_62976 and references mitigation testing in the VM13.0 ITP and ITR. D001597673 DFMEA VM13.0 GpuSignalPathImprovements links GPU-path failure modes to requirements such as VP2024_SRS-63544, VP2024_SRS-63546, and VP2024_SRS-63552 together with GPUBF ITP and ITR references. D001602384 VM13 DFMEA OneCollabLive links several failure modes to specific requirements and ITP or ITR execution references. | Summary: Feature DFMEAs provide surrogate evidence.  From the reviewed documents, no SW FMEA could be traced which comprehensively covers the risk of the software system. The referenced feature DFMEAs cover only newly added or modified features as part of VM13.0; inherited features from previous releases are not covered by these analyses. The term surrogate reflects the fact that meaningful software failure analysis does exist within the feature DFMEAs, but it is organized by feature scope rather than by software architecture, and therefore does not constitute systematic software-wide coverage.  Details: 1. No Dedicated SW FMEA or Equivalent Consolidated Software Failure-Analysis Method Was Identified, and Available Positive Evidence Is Surrogate Evidence Derived from Feature DFMEAs    - Evidence: The reviewed evidence consists of a set of feature-specific DFMEAs and the FRDR review of those DFMEAs. No single artifact was identified that defines a software-wide SW FMEA, software hazard-and-cause analysis, or equivalent method that systematically covers the software boundary as a whole. The software FMEA evidence comes from feature DFMEAs such as OnTheFlyForVm, EpmJson, GpuSignalPathImprovements, Static 3D Markers, Software Work For CV Optimization, and OneCollabLive, each of which contains software-relevant failure modes involving interface behavior, malformed inputs, processing overload, and internal interaction faults.    - Finding: The question is not fully answered because the evidence does not show a dedicated software-level failure-analysis framework.    - Why this is a finding: SW_4.1 is about SW failure analysis. Feature DFMEAs can support the answer only as surrogate evidence. Without a dedicated SW FMEA or an explicitly consolidated alternative method, the assessment remains incomplete.  2. VM13.0 Feature DFMEAs Do Not Cover Inherited Features from Prior Releases - Evidence: The FRDR (D001683707) scope states that it reviews "technical documentation and design created during the Detail Designs and Integrate Product phases of VM13.0." It lists exactly 11 feature DFMEAs, each scoped to a specific VM13.0 change proposal or feature improvement. The FRDR review feedback confirms inherited origins for example, Auto Measure V3 notes "we had AutoMeasure since VM9.0," GpuSignalPathImprovements notes "GPU signalpath was added since VM7.0," and EpmJson notes "we had binary EPM files in previous release." These comments acknowledge that existing failure analysis for those inherited functions exists in earlier-release DFMEAs, but those earlier DFMEAs are not part of the VM13.0 review. Why this is a finding: The available surrogate failure analysis evidence covers only the newly added or modified features as part of VM13.0. The broader software system — including core inherited functions such as imaging modes, Doppler processing, patient data management, DICOM connectivity, and measurement tools is not addressed by the VM13.0 feature DFMEAs.  This reinforces the characterization of the available evidence as surrogate rather than systematic. A dedicated software-wide failure analysis would by definition cover the full software boundary, including both new and inherited functionality. | Sample | Y | Y | SW_4.1 | [Qifeng] Agree with issue statements |  | Agree |  | Y | Y | Y |  |  | Y | H | N/A | See Compliance Rational on US legislation 21 CFR 820.30, column AC. | Adherence to IEC 62304 demonstrates compliance with general safety and performance requirements (GSPRs) |  |  |

Existing automated practices serve as functional regression (test-to-pass) rather than true robustness challenges, and System Verification occurs too late to satisfy the requirement for systematic and iterative robustness testing.  Details: 1. Absence of Test-to-Fail and Advanced Robustness Methodologies    - Evidence: A review of D001534058 Software Development Plan and D001550592 VM13.0 Reliability Plan reveals a reliance on daily automated regression testing (DART) and Automated System Tests (AST), but contains no procedural requirements for stress testing, load testing, test-to-fail, or mutation testing. Furthermore, D001984779 System Verification Report for VMQ13.0 contains zero references to the execution of "stress," "load," "robustness," or "test-to-fail" methodologies.    - Finding: The established automated systems (DART/AST) operate with a functional regression ("test-to-pass") intent. Neither the D001534058 Software Development Plan nor the D001550592 VM13.0 Reliability Plan demonstrate evidence of active testing methodologies designed specifically from a "test-to-fail" perspective to push systemic boundaries or induce software failure during development or formal verification.    - Why this is a finding: To systematically explore software robustness, testing strategies must include techniques intended to push the system beyond normal operating bounds or validate test effectiveness. Relying solely on functional regression does not satisfy the requirement for advanced robustness checks like stress, load, or mutation testing.  2. Lack of Systematic Execution During Design Development    - Evidence: Section 8.5 of D001534058 Software Development Plan documents the 72-hour AST longevity testing strictly as an "entry criteria for S-VER" (System Verification).    - Finding: Robustness testing must be performed systematically during the iterative design and development phases (check-and-optimize) to effectively identify and mitigate weaknesses. Executing longevity tests merely as a rigid, late-stage pre-condition for formal System Verification does not satisfy the expectation for regular robustness challenges throughout the development lifecycle.    - Why this is a finding: Waiting until formal verification to execute extended reliability tests limits the ability to iteratively discover and fix foundational architectural flaws during the active development loops. | Sample | Y | Y | SW_4.2 | [Qifeng] Agree with the findling, although there are the reliability suites AST that are continually executing during development isn’t written down in the Software Development Plan. |  | Agree |  | Y | Y | Y |  |  | Y | H | N/A | See Compliance Rational on US legislation 21 CFR 820.30, column AC. | Adherence to IEC 62304 demonstrates compliance with general safety and performance requirements (GSPRs) |  |  |

DFMEA Failure Modes Explicitly Mapped to RMM Risk IDs    Feature-level DFMEAs contain a dedicated "RMM ID" column that explicitly maps each safety-relevant software failure mode to a specific Risk ID in the Product Safety RMM, satisfying IEC 62304 Clause 7.3.3 traceability from software cause to hazardous situation.    - Evidence:      - D001597673 DFMEA GpuSignalPathImprovements, Row 1: Failure mode "Higher volume rates result in excessive CPU loading" → End effect "diagnostically significant volumes are potentially dropped... could lead to misdiagnosis" → RMM ID "MD-4050" (Misdiagnosis hazard category).      - D001597673 DFMEA GpuSignalPathImprovements, Row 2: Failure mode "volume rate higher than GPU can process, causing data overrun → system crash" → End effect "System not available, user needs to reboot, not acceptable with TEE probes" → RMM ID "MNA-01" (Machine Not Available hazard category).      - D001597673 DFMEA GpuSignalPathImprovements, Row 4: Failure mode "incorrect GPU kernel implementation causes out of bounds memory access → sometimes fatal CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS → BSOD" → RMM ID "MNA-01".  2. RMM Contains Explicit Hazardous Situations with Structured Harm Chains    D001572750 Product Safety RMM defines explicit hazardous situations per ISO 14971 format, including hazard category, hazardous situation, sequence of events, and enumerated harms. Each risk is assigned a unique Risk ID with initial severity/probability ratings.    - Evidence:      - Risk MD-01: Hazardous Situation = "Live or cineloop alignment error or single image review: shows e.g., blood flow where there shouldn't be, or heart shape at inappropriate points in cycle." Harm = "Anxiety, Distress, Injury, Misdiagnosis." Severity 3.      - Risk MNA-01: Hazardous Situation = "Machine not available due to a software failure; procedure must be redone or rescheduled (e.g., software lock-up, crash or software defect reducing functionality)." Harm = "Anxiety, Discomfort, Distress, Irritability." Severity 1.      - Risk A-01: Hazardous Situation = "Transducer is mis-used... leading to acoustic output that's higher than intended for the targeted anatomy." Harm = "Nerve Damage, Tissue Damage, Burn, Thermal." Severity 2.  3. Multiple Hazard Categories with Software-Related Traceability    The RMM covers software-related failure modes across multiple clinically distinct hazard categories. Software mitigations are flagged via a dedicated "SW-Related" column and classified A/B/C, enabling systematic identification of any software contribution to a hazard.    - Evidence of hazard categories with software-related mitigations reviewed:      - Misdiagnosis: MD-01 (alignment errors), MD-02 (alignment errors, lower severity), MD-10 (replay event alignment), MD-20 (replay user event), MD-30 (insufficient acquisition, data corruption), MD-35 (PW signal absent/compromised), MD-40 (defective transducer artifacts), MD-50 (defective pulse/phono transducers).      - Machine Not Available: MNA-01 (software failure causing system unavailability), MNA-02 (hardware damage/abuse), MNA-06 (hardware failure during non-interventional exams).      - Acoustic Power: A-01 (acoustic output higher than intended — ALARA controls, MI/TI display, output limits).      - Biopsy Guide: BG-20 (biopsy guide installed backwards — software warning), BG-50 (needle/guide path mismatch — software overlay accuracy). | Summary: The RMM contains software-related risk entries originating from legacy and prior-release failure analyses that fall outside the scope of the VM13.0 feature DFMEAs reviewed. Details: 1. Peer Review as Part of the Development Process The D001534058 Software Development Plan describes a peer review gate for unit-level work products. The Test Plan/Procedure for each Change Set Document is reviewed before implementation, and the design and test plan must be peer review approved before the developer proceeds to implement.    - Evidence: D001534058, Section "Unit Software Development Plan and Test": "The Test Plan/Procedure is part of the peer review process as shown." and "Once the design and test plan are peer review approved the developer proceeds to implement the same and completed executing the test plan."  2. Daily Automated Regression Testing via DART The D001534058 Software Development Plan establishes Daily Automated Regression Tests as a standing practice integrated into continuous integration. Automated unit tests are executed daily as part of this framework, providing a systematic regression baseline throughout the development phase.    - Evidence: D001534058, Section "Unit Software Development Plan and Test": "There are Automated Unit tests that are executed Daily as part of the Automated test Framework and these tests are run as part of the DART (Daily Automated Regression tests)."    - Evidence: D001534058, Appendix 1 (Reliability Plan), Section "Reliability Activities": "DART (Daily Automated regression tests) are part of the development to monitor SW reliability. DART are run daily and is part of the continuous integration process. DART monitors the quality of daily check-ins."  3. Multi-Level Testing Strategy The D001534058 Software Development Plan and D001881563 System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0 together describe verification activities across three levels. Unit tests are captured within individual Change Set Documents. Feature-level integration testing is documented via Integration Test Plans and Integration Test Reports managed in configuration management. System-level verification is governed by the D001881563 System Verification Plan, which includes black-box testing, automated system tests (AST), localization verification, white-box verification via IntegDev Test Plans, and security scans.    - Evidence: D001534058, Section "Integration Test": "Prior to MVP the feature owners create an Integration Test Plan (ITP). The Integration test plan is executed by an independent developer and the results of the test execution are captured in an Integration Test Report."    - Evidence: D001881563, Section "Test Design": "The requirements that the System Verification group is responsible are covered in the test activities listed in Appendix A." and "The Automated System Test group are responsible for executing automated test suites that evaluate the stability of the software under test."    - Evidence: D001881563, Section "Test Design - White Box Verification": references VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan and QLAB 15.8.3 Measurement Verification IntegDev Test Plan for requirements that cannot be verified in a black-box manner.    - Evidence: DM181L181 | Summary: Neither the D001534058 Software Development Plan nor the D001881563 System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0 functions as a dedicated software verification plan as defined by IEC 62304 Clause 5.1.6. The D001897907 VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan functions as a verification plan for a specific subset of risk-mitigating requirements requiring white-box verification, but does not address software-wide verification practices. In the absence of a dedicated software verification plan, the following findings identify elements expected under this question that are not addressed by any of the reviewed documents.  Details: 1. No Dedicated Software Verification Plan    - Evidence: The D001534058 Software Development Plan contains a "Verification" section that states: "The Formal Product Verification Plan for VM 13.0 will be created prior to the SVER-R milestone. The verification of the software will be part of the overall system verification." The D001881563 is titled "System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0" and scopes itself to system-level requirement verification.    - Finding: No document titled or functioning as a Software Verification Plan consolidating all software-specific verification practices was identified in the reviewed documentation. The SDP defers verification planning to a "Formal Product Verification Plan" and to the System Verification Plan. The System Verification Plan addresses system-level requirements verification, sample-size determination, and hardware configuration coverage. The D001897907 VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan provides white-box verification procedures for a subset of risk-mitigating requirements but does not address software-wide verification practices such as coding standards, code review mandates, or static analysis requirements.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 Clause 5.1.6 requires that the manufacturer "plan the software verification tasks including the milestones at which the verification tasks are to be completed." A software verification plan is expected to consolidate the strategies, methods, and tools for verifying software units, integration, and system testing. Distributing these elements across a development plan and a system verification plan without a consolidating software-level plan creates gaps in coverage, particularly for software-specific practices.  2. No Essential Design Output-Specific Testing Strategy or Exhaustive Testing Methodologies    - Evidence: Neither the D001534058 Software Development Plan, the D001881563 System Verification Plan, nor the D001897907 VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan contains any reference to property-based testing, mutation testing, performance testing, fuzzy testing, chaos testing, or other exhaustive testing methodologies. The D001897907 VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan includes fault injection and boundary testing for specific risk-mitigating requirements, but this is requirement-driven verification for a defined subset rather than a systematic exhaustive testing strategy applied to all Essential Design Output requirements. No document describes a differentiated testing strategy for requirements related to Essential Design Outputs, where enhanced rigor or expanded input coverage would be applied across CtQ, CtS, essential performance, and basic safety categories. No reference to pair programming as a development practice appears in any of the reviewed documents.    - Finding: The testing strategy treats all requirements uniformly through the same unit/integration/system pipeline without a documented escalation of rigor for EDO-related requirements. Essential Design Outputs encompass not only CtQ and CtS requirements but also essential performance and basic safety requirements; no differentiated verification approach exists for any of these categories. No exhaustive or adversarial testing approach is described to challenge the software with a wide range of random input parameters. Additionally, pair programming is not documented as a practice in any of the reviewed planning documents.    - Why this is a finding: "By testing an exhaustive range of parameters unexpected behaviors and errors in the field can be prevented." The guidance also expects pair programming or independent review as part of the mature coding practice set. Without differentiated EDO testing covering CtQ, CtS, essential performance, and basic safety requirements, without exhaustive testing methodologies, and without pair programming as a documented practice, the verification strategy does not demonstrate that safety-critical and effectiveness-critical software paths receive the enhanced scrutiny expected for a Class C software system.  3. No Evidence of Static or Dynamic Analysis Tooling    - Evidence: No reference to static analysis tools (e.g., Coverity, SonarQube, PC-lint), dynamic analysis tools, code coverage measurement tools, linting tools, or automated code quality enforcement mechanisms was found in D001534058 Software Development Plan, D001881563 System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0, or D001897907 VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan. A mention of "Static Code Analysis" appears in D001569454 Product Security Risk Assessment in the context of security vulnerability identification, but this is security-scoped and not indicative of a systematic development practice mandated by a verification plan. No code coverage targets or measurement methodology is defined for unit tests or integration tests in any of the reviewed documents.    - Finding: The reviewed documentation does not demonstrate that static analysis, dynamic analysis, or code coverage measurement is requested or mandated as part of the software verification strategy. Neither the D001534058 Software Development Plan nor the D001881563 System Verification Plan defines coverage targets for unit testing or integration testing, nor documents a mechanism for measuring or reporting code coverage.    - Why this is a finding: The Assessment Matrix guidance expects mature coding practices to include at minimum "CI/CD, dynamic analysis, static analysis, coding style, pair programming/independent review, unit test/integration test code coverage." The absence of documented analysis tooling and code coverage metrics means there is no verifiable mechanism to systematically detect common defect patterns, memory safety violations, or unreachable code, and no documented basis to assess whether unit and integration tests adequately cover the implemented code paths.  4. No Named Coding Standard    - Evidence: A comprehensive search of D001534058 Software Development Plan, D001881563 System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0, and D001897907 VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan found no reference to any named coding standard such as MISRA C, MISRA C++, CERT C, PEP 8, or a formally documented proprietary standard. The D001534058 "Detailed design acceptance Criteria" section lists design review criteria for Class C components but these are architectural review considerations, not coding-level rules governing syntax, style, or known language hazard patterns.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 Clause 5.5.3 requires establishing strategies, methods, and procedures for verifying software units, which includes the adoption of coding standards to prevent language-specific hazards. The pass/fail criteria for this question expect the verification plan to explicitly name the coding standard used. Without a named or referenced standard, there is no documented basis to enforce or verify coding discipline.  5. Code Review Scope Limited to Design and Test Plans    - Evidence: The D001534058 Software Development Plan describes peer review for design and test plan artifacts within the CSD process: "The Test Plan/Procedure is part of the peer review process" and "Once the design and test plan are peer review approved the developer proceeds to implement." No statement mandates peer review of actual production source code before merging into the main branch.    - Finding: The documented peer review process covers the test plan/procedure and design within each Change Set Document. However, there is no documented mandate that production source code itself is reviewed by an independent peer before being committed or merged. The D001534058 Software Development Plan states that "Software developers may directly deliver their code to the main software branch," with no stated requirement for code review prior to delivery.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 Clause 5.5.5 requires verification of software units against their detailed design, with code review being a recognized method. The expectation under this question is that the verification plan mandates code review for production code to ensure correctness, safety-relevant implementation quality, and the presence of identifiers marking code parts that implement a CtQ or CtS. The chosen review method should enable tracing from the code back to the specific CtQ or CtS being implemented. Reviewing only the test plan and design, without reviewing the implementing code itself, means there is no documented mechanism to verify that CtQ/CtS-implementing code paths are correctly identified, marked, and traceable. | Sample | Y | Y | SW_5.1 | [Qifeng] Agree there is no dedicated SW Verification  plan. SRS-to-architecture/design, source-code-to-design, and all reverse-direction chains are not addressed by any controlled document in the reviewed set. The remaining elements are addressed in the Issue Analysis Statement.  Details: 1. IntegDev Test Plan requirement-to-test-step mapping with risk-mitigating flags    - Evidence: The D001897907 VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan contains tabulated SRS-to-test-step mapping: "VP2024_SRS-46414 | The output power adjustable range is from the maximum allowed value as specified in the applicable regulatory standards for the current system state, to a minimum value which is transducer and TSP dependent | Test Step 5.5 | OCS | Risk Mitigating: Yes." | Summary: The reviewed documents present three categories of findings. First, D001534058 Software Development Plan plans only SW requirements-to-verification-test traceability and omits architecture, design, and code trace chains required for Class C systems. Second, D001750035 Voyager System Design Specification explicitly disclaims traceability between subsystem design and SW requirements, no DHF-controlled document mandates how source code traceability is managed, bidirectionality is not demonstrated, and no orphan analysis is performed. Third, SW requirements-to-test traceability resides in DOORS rather than in DHF-controlled documentation, and the verification plan and report do not provide requirement-to-test-to-verdict mapping.  Details:  1. SDP traceability plan omits architecture and design trace chains     - Evidence: The D001534058 Software Development Plan Section "Traceability" plans SW requirements-to-verification-test and risk-to-SW-requirements-to-verification chains only. URS-to-SRS is also planned but outside the scope of this question. No trace chain involving software architecture, detailed design, or source code is included.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 Clause 5.1.1 requires the plan to address traceability for software architecture, detailed design, and software units for Class C systems. Table A.1 mandates Clauses 5.3.6, 5.4.4, and 5.5.5 at this classification. Under FDA 2005 guidance, Class C corresponds to Major level of concern; under FDA 2023 guidance, Enhanced documentation level applies, requiring independently auditable traceability across all V-model phases.  2. System Design Specification explicitly disclaims traceability to SW requirements    - Evidence: The D001750035 Voyager System Design Specification Section 5.2 states: "the functional partition and resulting subsystem design requirements are not traceable directly to the SRS or any regulatory standard. Instead, they are largely a reflection of Ultrasound's overall strategic objectives for our product line."    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 Clause 5.3.6 requires verification that the software architecture implements the software requirements for Class B and C systems.  3. No DHF-controlled document mandates how source code traceability is managed    - Evidence: The D001534058 Software Development Plan does not include source code in any planned traceability chain and does not define a mandatory process for linking code commits to design or requirements. The D001707530 Voyager Software Platform Design Specification contains informal SW requirements references but does not establish formal code-to-design linkage or mandate a traceability mechanism.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 Clauses 5.5.5 and 5.4.4 require verification that software units implement the detailed design and that detailed design implements the architecture for Class C systems. The expectation is that a DHF-controlled document defines mandatory instructions for how code-to-requirement traceability is implemented, not that it occurs on a voluntary basis by individual engineers.  4. Bidirectionality not demonstrated in any trace chain    - Evidence: The D001534058 Software Development Plan, D001881563 System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0, and D001897907 VM13.0 IntegDev Test Plan each document forward-direction traces only (SW requirements to test, requirements to test steps). No reverse-direction trace generation is described or demonstrated.    - Why this is a finding: The question requires "and vice versa" for each linkage. IEC 62304 Clauses 5.2.6, 5.3.6, 5.4.4, and 5.5.5 require conformance in both directions.  5. SW requirements-to-test traceability resides in DOORS, not in DHF-controlled documentation    - Evidence: The D001881563 System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0 states: "Traceability between tests and the system level requirements will be maintained in IBM Rational DOORS." The D002026780 System Verification Traceability Matrix for VMQ13.0 lists DOORS baseline identifiers and PTC Windchill references but contains no exported trace data, matrix rows, or linkage examples. The documents in DOORS are the latest baseline release for the VMQ13.0 requirements and is considered the master version of the System Requirements and all System Verification evidences are added as part of the "SVV VM13.0 Non-SVV Test Reference" attribute.    - Why this is a finding: IEC 62304 Clauses 5.7.4 and 5.7.5 require verification that test coverage addresses all software requirements. The DHF document designated for this purpose (D002026780) contains no trace data — it is a pointer to DOORS baselines. Because DOORS is a live tool database and not a controlled DHF artifact, the traceability required by these clauses cannot be independently verified from the DHF.  6. DOORS export shows requirements with blank verification test reference    - Evidence: Analysis of the DOORS baseline export for Voyager SRS reveals requirements have a blank "SVV VM13.0 Non-SVV Test Reference" column. For example, VP2024_SRS-60038 has no SVV test reference assigned. The blank entries represent a coverage gap that prevents confirmation of complete requirement-to-test traceability within DOORS itself. Additionally, inconsistencies exist between the requirements documented in the formal requirement specification documents (e.g., D001750035 Voyager System Design Specification) and the requirements captured in the DOORS export, further complicating traceability verification.    - Why this is a finding: Even within DOORS — which is the only location where requirement-to-test traceability is maintained (see Detail 5) — blank SVV test references indicate that not all requirements have been linked to verification evidence. IEC 62304 Clause 5.7.4 requires complete test coverage of software requirements. A coverage gap in the only traceability mechanism means completeness cannot be confirmed.  7. Verification protocol does not provide requirement-to-test-case-to-verdict mapping    - Evidence: The D001881563 System Verification Plan for VMQ13.0 does not contain a tabulated mapping of requirement identifiers to test protocol identifiers and test verdicts. The D001984779 System Verification Report for VMQ13.0 references D002026780 for traceability but does not itself include a requirement-to-test-to-verdict matrix. The expected traceability chain for system verification is at minimum: requirement → verification protocol → verification record. VER_4.6 confirms that the D001898913 System Verification Test Protocol for VMQ13.0 contains test procedures but "link between each of these procedures and tested requirements could not be established. Therefore, no traceability could be found."    - Why this is a finding: Explicit traceability between requirement ID, test protocol ID, and test verdict is expected in the verification plan/report or a separate trace matrix, per IEC 62304 Clauses 5.7.4 and 5.7.5. The D001898913 test protocol contains procedures without requirement linkage, confirming that the traceability chain breaks at the protocol level. | Sample | Y | Y | SW_6.1 | [Qifeng] Agree with issue statements |  | Agree |  | Y | Y | Y |  |  | Y | H | N/A | Traceability analyses is one of several verification activities that confirms by objective evidence that the output of a particular phase of development meets all the input requirements for that phase. Quality System Regulation (QSR): The FDA has transitioned from the legacy QSR to the new QMSR, aligning with ISO 13485:2016 to enhance global consistency for medical device manufacturers. |  | Cybersecurity management plans should include the following elements:  • Personnel responsible;  • Sources, methods, and frequency for monitoring and identifying vulnerabilities (e.g., researchers, NIST national vulnerability database (NIST NVD), third-party software manufacturers);  • Identify and address vulnerabilities identified in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog • Periodic security testing; • Timeline to develop and release patches;  • Update processes; • Patching capability (i.e., rate at which update can be delivered to devices);  • Description of their coordinated vulnerability disclosure process; and • Description of how the manufacturer intends to communicate forthcoming remediations,  patches, and updates to customers.  Recommended 510(k) Submission Documentation 1. Cybersecurity Risk Management Report   a. Threat Model (may include Architecture Views)   b. Cybersecurity Risk Assessment   c. SBOM   d. Vulnerability Assessment and Software Support   e. Unresolved Anomalies Assessment   f. Traceability Demonstrates the traceability between device cybersecurity risks and controls. Adequate cybersecurity traceability documentation is important to comply with the requirements speci􀏐ied in section 524B(b)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to provide a reasonable assurance that the device and related systems are cybersecure. It is also consistent with the recommendations in Section 6 of the FDA guidance “Content of Premarket Submissions for Management of Cybersecurity in Medical Devices” (https://www.fda.gov/media/86174/download) to provide a traceability matrix that links your actual cybersecurity controls to the cybersecurity risks that were considered."  2. Measures and Metrics 3. Architecture Views   a. Requirements   b. Architecture Views (may be included in Threat Model) 4. Testing Cybersecurity Testing Cybersecurity controls require testing beyond standard software verification and validation activities to demonstrate the effectiveness of the controls in a proper security context to therefore demonstrate that the device has a reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness. Under 21 CFR 820.30(f), a manufacturer must establish and maintain procedures for verifying the device design. Such verification shall confirm that the design output meets the design input requirements. Under 21 CFR 820.30(g), a manufacturer must establish and maintain procedures for validating its device design. Such design validation shall include software validation and risk analysis, where appropriate. FDA recommends verification and validation include sufficient testing performed by the manufacturer on the cybersecurity of the medical device system through which the manufacturer verifies and validates their inputs and outputs, as appropriate. 5. Labeling 6. Cybersecurity Management Plans (Section 524B of the FD&C Act requires the submission of certain documentation for cyber devices in order for manufacturers to meet their obligations for what is required to be in premarket submissions under section 524B.  Section 524B(b)(1) of the FD&C Act requires manufacturers of cyber devices to submit to FDA a plan to monitor, identify, and address, as appropriate, in a reasonable time, postmarket cybersecurity vulnerabilities and exploits, including coordinated vulnerability disclosure and related procedures” in their premarket submissions.) |  |

## Sheet: Glossary

| Term | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| consistent | Related information which is not conflicting, e.g. : ·       similar information used in different artefacts shall be the same ·       derived information shall be not conflicting with the source |
| critical task | A user task which, if performed incorrectly or not performed at all, would or could cause serious harm to the patient or user, where harm is defined to include compromised medical care. |
| load case | refers to a documented environmental condition, use profile or a set or combination of these, under which the performance of a function is required to be delivered |
| serious harm | refers to a harm level S4 OR S3 (per definition in the risk acceptability policy), OR S2 (harm serious enough to be considered critical to safety by a qualified medical affairs representative) |
| test case | A test case in the context of design verification is a test description on a specific aspect of a function, e.g. accuracy of positioning system of the test tool |
| test method | A test method in the context of design verification is a specific technical procedure for performing test, e.g. measure of a distance with specified means |
| user | Anybody that operates or interacts with the product in the course of the life cycle of the product (in line with IEC 62366 definition) |
